extracted.intended_audience: students and educated general readers of philosophy, social theory, and the history of ideas
extracted.subtask_description: Close critical reading and evaluation of Plato's proposals about property, marriage, and sex roles (as discussed by a later commentator). Identifies standards and objections used to judge the desirability, practicability, and moral consequences of such social institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property legitimacy based on expediency
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of private property is based on expediency, and may be interfered with in a variety of ways for the public good; 'the most useful... would be the most sacred.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that legal and ecclesiastical talk of property as 'sacred' really aimed to resist invasion of individual rights; a form of vesting which is proved more advantageous would in time acquire the same basis of right. Use utility/public good as the touchstone of property institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community of property undermines incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Motives for exertion would be taken away under a community of property; 'Every man would produce as little and consume as much as he liked.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections (from Aristotle and the essay) stress loss of individual incentive and disputes caused by collective dependence; experience of civilized nations has generally been adverse to Socialism because 'personal feeling is always breaking in.' Evaluate proposals for communal property by their effects on productivity and individual motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions judged by potential to raise general culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribution of wealth should be evaluated by whether it is 'most favourable that can be conceived for the education and development of the mass of mankind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentator allows that property arrangements could change if they better promoted public education and culture; comparisons to historical changes (abolition of slavery, emancipation of serfs, rapid modernization) are used to show institutions can evolve toward greater public benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender equality claims must weigh nature and education
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato's denial of organic difference between men and women is contestable; differences may affect whole nature but may also be substantially due to education and inherited habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposals for equal roles of sexes by considering evidence about physical vs social origins of sex differences, the plasticity of bodily/psychological traits over generations, and variation across countries and classes; do not assume either absolute biological determinism or pure social construction without argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community of wives destroys higher human qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato's proposal for a community of wives and children would banish sentiment, imagination, and the poetic aspects of love—reducing human relations to animalistic arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that arranging marriage solely to improve the race eliminates affectionate ties and the 'world of poetry and fancy' that love produces; evaluate such reforms for their effects on human affections, moral sentiments, and cultural life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breeding policies dehumanize and neglect mind/character
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting the 'best' for breeding and destroying the others treats humans like animals and overlooks the intellectual and moral qualities that constitute human excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentator insists improvement of the human race consists in growth and enlightenment of the mind, not merely physical attributes. Policies aimed only at bodily traits risk producing brutish outcomes and losing imagination, reason, and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family structures are necessary for child welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: A system in which all children are state foundlings would cause high mortality and fail to supply the 'subtle sympathy between the mother and the child' that private families provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical concerns about infant survival and psychological bonds to judge proposals that abolish family child-rearing (e.g., creches, foundling systems); the essay cites historical examples (Paris creches, Dublin foundling hospital) to argue such systems are often fatal to many children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect individuality to foster genius and progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems that smother individuality extinguish the emergence of remarkable individuals, which are the source of political, artistic, and scientific progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Spartan example is used to show that political arrangements which subordinate the individual to the state suppress talents (no Themistocles, Pericles, Aeschylus, etc.). Evaluate social designs by their capacity to allow 'scattered seeds or sparks of genius' to appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't overapply animal analogies to human social policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies drawn from animal breeding or behaviour mislead when applied to humans because they ignore those qualities (mind, conscience, imagination) which distinguish humans from animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that treating humans as breeders' stock overlooks moral and mental dimensions; any policy modeled on animal practices must be scrutinized for its inapplicability to human ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heredity should inform prudence in marriage decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge that certain vices or diseases run in a family (drunkenness, insanity, consumption) ought to guide marriage decisions and sometimes counsel avoidance of marriage as a duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay gives examples of men who avoided marriage because of hereditary disease. Use heredity as a factor to prevent avoidable suffering, while recognizing limits of certainty and need to balance feeling and propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population and timing of marriage affect communal welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Imprudence in marriage among the poor (too early marriage, overpopulation) hinders amelioration of poverty and produces sickly, underdeveloped offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy solutions might be indirect (education, emigration, agricultural and industrial improvements). Evaluate marriage-related norms for their demographic and economic consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculations on origins can unsettle but must be handled morally
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing that institutions like marriage grew from history and selfish beginnings may be unsettling; such inquiries risk undermining moral sentiment in times of transition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing reforms or exposing historical origins, weigh the danger of weakening moral restraints and of providing excuses for 'listening to the voice of passion' under the guise of new knowledge or novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and intellectual goods outrank purely physical considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where physical or biological explanations exist, reason, conscience, duty, and truth remain primary; health of body depends on health of mind and moral sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce virtue to physical health or merely biological terms; social policies must account for the primacy of moral and intellectual development alongside physical well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain sacredness of institutions when utility supports it
rubrics_metrics.description: There is more reason to maintain the sacredness of marriage when its benefits to society are evident rather than merely by vague religious horror; 'that which is the most holy will be the most useful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demonstrable public benefits to justify protecting or consecrating institutions; the argument links utility to the basis of reverence and social protection.
